subject: Vocabulary
description: Common scientific / academic roots — derm, hydro, photo, geo, therm, helio, micro, macro

questions.stem: The root 'HYDRO-' (as in hydrology, hydraulic, hydrogen) means:
questions.explanation: HYDRO- (Greek 'hydor' = water). Hydrology — study of water. Hydraulic — water-pressure-based. Hydrogen — water-former (H + O₂ → H₂O). Hydroelectricity — electricity from flowing water. Dehydrate — remove water. Hydrophobia — fear of water (rabies symptom). Anhydrous — without water (chemistry).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.explanation: PHOTO- (Greek 'phos / photos' = light). Photograph — light-drawn picture. Photosynthesis — light-based food synthesis (plants). Photon — particle of light. Phototropism — growth toward light. Phototherapy — light-based treatment (e.g., for jaundice). Photoelectric — electricity by light. Photovoltaic — light → voltage. Compare PHONO- (sound — phonograph, telephone, symphony, phoneme); CHRONO- (time — chronology, chronic, synchronous, chronometer); CHROMO- / CHROM- (colour — chromosome, chromatic, monochrome, photochromic).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: The root 'DERM-' / 'DERMA-' (as in dermatology, epidermis, hypodermic) refers to:
questions.explanation: DERM- (Greek 'derma' = skin). Dermatology — skin medicine. Epidermis — outer skin layer (Greek epi = upon). Hypodermic — under skin (hypo = under). Dermatitis — skin inflammation. Pachyderm — thick-skinned (elephants, rhinos). Compare other body-part roots: OS / OSTEO (bone — osteoporosis, osteopathy); CARDIO (heart — cardiology, cardiac, cardiogram); HAEMO / HEMA (blood — haemoglobin, hemorrhage); NEPH(R)O (kidney — nephritis, nephron); HEPATO (liver); CYTO (cell — cytology, cytoplasm); NEURO (nerve — neurology, neuron).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Match prefix to meaning — which is INCORRECT?
questions.explanation: MONO- means ONE, not many. Monogamy = marriage to one partner; monosyllable; monorail; monolith; monologue. Compare POLY- (many: polygamy, polyglot, polyhedron). DI- / DUO- (two: dialogue [actually 'between two'], dioxide, duo). TRI- (three). MICRO- (small: microscope, microbe, microchip). MACRO- (large: macroscope rare, macroeconomics, macrocosm). GEO- (earth: geology, geography, geocentric, geomorphology). BIO- (life: biology, biography, antibiotic).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: The root 'THERM-' (as in thermostat, thermal, thermos, thermometer) means:
questions.explanation: THERM- (Greek 'therme' = heat). Thermometer — heat measurer. Thermostat — heat regulator. Thermal — relating to heat. Thermos — insulated flask (Sir James Dewar, 1892). Hyperthermia (heatstroke). Hypothermia (low body temperature). Thermodynamics — physics of heat. Endothermic / Exothermic — absorbing / releasing heat. Compare 'cold' roots: CRYO- (cryogenic, cryptobiosis); GLAC- (glacier, glaciate). 'Time' roots: CHRONO- (chronology); 'Sound': PHONO-, ACOUSTI- (acoustics).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.explanation: ASTRO- (Greek 'astron'). Astrology — star-influence belief. Astronomy — star-laws (the science). Asterisk — little star (the * symbol). Astronaut — star-sailor. Disaster — DIS (bad) + aster (star) = ill-starred. STELLAR (Latin) — relating to stars (e.g., constellation, interstellar). Other space-related roots: COSM- (universe — cosmos, cosmonaut, microcosm, cosmopolitan); LUNA- (moon — lunatic, lunar); SOL- (sun — solar, parasol).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.explanation: GRAPH- (Greek 'graphein' = to write/draw). Graphology — analysis of handwriting. Geography — earth-writing / description of earth. Photography — light-drawing. Bibliography — list of books written. Autograph — self-signature. Telegraph — far-writing. Cartography — map-making. Calligraphy — beautiful writing. Compare LOG- (speech / word — logic, logo, prologue, dialogue, biology); LEG- / LECT- (read — legible, lecture); GRAM- (also writing/letter — gram, grammar, telegram, anagram, monogram).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: The Latin root 'BENE-' (found in benefactor, benevolent, and benediction) carries which core meaning?

options.option_text: related to force, power, or physical strength
related to goodness, well-being, or benefit
related to life, living organisms, or biology
related to harm, danger, or destructive intent

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'BENE-' comes from Latin 'bonus/bene' meaning good or well — a benefactor is one who does good, benevolent means wishing good. Option C is wrong because 'life/living organisms' maps to roots like 'BIO-' or 'VIT-', not 'BENE-'. Option D (harm) is the near-opposite; that root would be 'MAL-' (malevolent, malefactor).

questions.stem: The Latin root 'MORT-' / 'MORI-' (as in mortal, mortuary, and immortal) is fundamentally connected to which concept?

options.option_text: movement, travel, or physical displacement in space
darkness, shadow, or absence of visible light
death, dying, or the state of being perishable
suffering, pain, or enduring physical injury

questions.explanation: C is correct: 'MORT-' derives from Latin 'mors/mortis' (death) — mortal means subject to death, mortuary is a place for the dead, immortal means not subject to death. Option D (suffering/pain) is a common confusion; pain-related roots include 'DOLOR-' (dolorous) or 'PATH-' (pathology). Option A (movement) maps to 'MOT-' / 'MOB-', a root students frequently mix up with 'MORT-'.

questions.stem: The Greek root 'CHRON-' (as in chronology, chronicle, and synchronize) carries which core meaning?

options.option_text: relating to colour, pigmentation, or light spectrum properties
relating to time, duration, or the sequence of events
relating to sound, audio frequency, or acoustic vibration
relating to physical space, area, or three-dimensional volume

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'CHRON-' comes from Greek 'chronos' (time) — chronology orders events in time, synchronize means to make happen at the same time, an anachronism is something out of its correct time period. Option A is the most tempting trap: 'CHROM-' (not 'CHRON-') means colour, as in chromosome and chromatic; exam setters frequently exploit this one-letter difference to catch careless readers.

questions.stem: In the word 'CIRCUMLOCUTION' (expressing something in roundabout words), the root 'LOCUT-' derives from Latin 'loqui', meaning what?

options.option_text: to circle around or move repeatedly in a loop
to speak, talk, or express oneself in words
to write, inscribe, or formally record information
to hide, conceal, or keep something from others

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'LOCUT-' / 'LOQU-' comes from Latin 'loqui' (to speak) — loquacious means talkative, eloquent means speaking fluently, ventriloquist is one who speaks (seems to speak) from the belly. Option A is wrong; 'CIRCUM-' (around) is the prefix here, not the root — students misattribute meaning to the wrong morpheme. Option C (write/record) belongs to roots like 'SCRIB-' / 'SCRIPT-'.

questions.stem: Three of these words share a Latin or Greek root meaning 'life'. Which is the ODD ONE OUT?

options.option_text: vivacious — full of life, lively, and enthusiastic in manner
biography — a written account of someone's life and history
vitality — the state of having abundant physical energy or life
omnivore — an organism consuming both plant and animal matter

questions.explanation: D is correct: 'omnivore' contains 'OMNI-' (all) + 'VORE-' (to eat/devour) — neither root means 'life'. The other three all carry a life root: 'vivacious' has 'VIV-' (Latin vivere, to live), 'biography' has 'BIO-' (Greek bios, life), and 'vitality' has 'VIT-' (Latin vita, life). This distractor traps students who focus on the word's association with living organisms rather than its actual etymology.

questions.stem: Which of the following root-meaning pairs is INCORRECTLY matched?

options.option_text: 'GREG-' (as in gregarious, aggregate) — meaning 'flock or group'
'LUMIN-' (as in luminous, illuminate) — meaning 'shadow or darkness'

questions.explanation: B is incorrect: 'LUMIN-' derives from Latin 'lumen/luminis' meaning LIGHT, not shadow — luminous means emitting light, illuminate means to light up. The root for shadow or shade is 'UMBR-' (umbra, umbrella, adumbrate). Options A, C, and D are all correctly matched: 'GREG-' (grex = flock), 'CORP-' (corpus = body), and 'SENT-/SENS-' (sentire = to feel/perceive) are standard etymology that competitive papers regularly verify.

questions.stem: The word 'MAGNANIMOUS' is built from Latin 'magnus' (great) and 'animus' (spirit/mind). Which option accurately captures its meaning?

options.option_text: physically large, imposing, and commanding a grand presence
generously noble in spirit, free from petty resentment or spite
possessed of great intellectual brilliance and wide learning
prone to exaggerating personal achievements or boasting of greatness

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'magnanimous' literally means 'great of spirit' — it describes someone who is noble, forgiving, and rises above pettiness, especially toward a defeated rival. Option A is the most seductive trap: 'magnus' does mean great, but the greatness here is of spirit ('animus'), not physical stature. Option D (boastful) is the near-antonym; true magnanimity is quiet nobility, not self-promotion. Option C conflates 'great spirit' with intellectual greatness, which would be closer to 'genius' (from Latin 'ingenium').
